facts.strongest_angle: LEAD WITH THE PERMIT, AND SELL THE PAPERWORK AS THE PRODUCT. In Sunset Beach, adding more than 200 square feet of impervious surface triggers a town stormwater management plan that must be designed by a licensed professional and signed off after construction before occupancy — but the UDO also provides an escape hatch almost nobody in this market knows about: alternative materials can be excluded from the impervious definition entirely with a sealed letter from a North Carolina professional engineer certifying hydraulic conductivity of 1.41 inches per hour or greater. So the headline is roughly: 'In Sunset Beach, a turf yard over 200 square feet is a permit question before it is a landscaping question — and we build systems that certify pervious at 1.41 in/hr, with the sealed PE letter in your file.' Follow it with the three other constraints that competitors will get wrong on this island: solid plastic underlayment is flatly prohibited, recycled tire and rubberised products are barred from the island zoning districts and within 30 feet of water, and any fence facing the ocean, waterway, marsh or a golf course is capped at four feet and must be at least 50% transparent. Then the demographic close: 60.1% of residents are over 65 and 55.1% of housing units sit vacant much of the year, so the emotional proposition is 'your yard looks identical in February when you are not here,' sold to an absentee owner who needs to approve work remotely. WHY THIS DIFFERS FROM ITS NEIGHBOURS: Shallotte's threshold is an acre and its buyer is a working family — the permit story does not exist there. Carolina Shores has no waterfront, no CAMA, and its gatekeeper is a private ARC board. Calabash's buyer is a restaurant. Sunset Beach is the only one of the four where a barrier island, a CAMA Area of Environmental Concern, a hard 45% impervious cap and a named engineering standard all land on the same job — and the only one where the correct lead is regulatory competence rather than lifestyle.
facts.ordinance_or_hoa: BY FAR THE MOST TURF-SPECIFIC CODE IN THE BATCH — this town's page should be built on it. All from the Town of Sunset Beach Unified Development Ordinance (2023 working copy on the town's own server). (1) THE 200-SQUARE-FOOT TRIGGER: 'A stormwater management plan shall be required prior to the issuance of any permits for new construction or renovation/expansion projects where the impervious surface coverage increases by greater than 200 square feet.' That plan must be designed by a professional engineer, registered landscape architect or licensed surveyor, and must be inspected and approved after construction by that professional before a certificate of occupancy. Compare Shallotte's one-acre trigger. (2) THE PE LETTER — THE SINGLE MOST VALUABLE FINDING IN THIS BATCH. The UDO defines Impervious Surface as 'any surface which in whole or in part, restricts or prevents the natural absorption of water into the ground,' lists specific pervious exceptions (uncovered wooden slatted decks; the water area of a swimming pool; No. 57 stone at least four inches thick over geotextile fabric; certain trails), and then provides an open door: 'Alternative materials, not subject to the definition of impervious surface, may be proposed subject to certification of a licensed and certified North Carolina professional engineer of compliance with the hydraulic conductivity standard of 1.41 inches per hour or greater. Such certification shall be in the form of a letter under seal.' In plain terms: a properly built turf system CAN be classified as pervious in Sunset Beach, but only with a sealed NC PE letter at 1.41 in/hr or better. That is a service, and it is a moat. (3) IMPERVIOUS CAPS: residential development (single-family and duplex) may not exceed 45% impervious surface of total lot area; in the CR-1 (Conservation Reserve), CR-2 (Conservation Preservation) and AF-1 (Agricultural-Forestry) districts, not more than 20%. (4) SOLID PLASTIC BANNED: 'Only landscaping fabric which allows rain water to flow through is permitted. Solid plastic cover is prohibited.' (5) RUBBER RESTRICTED: non-biodegradable manmade mulch, explicitly including 'recycled tire mulch and other rubberized products,' may not be located in the BR-1, BR-2, BB-1 or CR-1 zoning districts, may not be used within the Limit of Moderate Wave Action, may not be placed within 30 feet of a water body, and must sit inside a border at least six inches higher than the material. That reaches crumb-rubber infill and rubber playground surfacing on the island. (6) FENCES (pet turf): island residential districts BR-1, BR-2 and CR-1 cap fences at four feet; mainland residential districts allow six; and any fence facing the ocean, waterway, marsh, lakes or a golf course 'may not exceed four (4) feet in height and shall be at least 50% transparent.' Chain link is allowed only in the rear yard and may not extend past the front footprint of the principal structure. Installing a fence requires a minor site plan. (7) DUNES: frontal dunes are exempt from the landscaping requirements, but owners of properties with primary frontal dunes 'shall plant approved vegetation on at least 25% of the frontal dune area' — American Beach Grass, Sea Oats, Seashore Elder, Bitter Panicum, Spartina patens. Turf stops at the dune line. (8) GROUND COVER is mandatory on all portions of exposed ground not occupied by other approved landscape material. (9) TREES: regulated and heritage trees are protected (live oak, pond cypress, bald cypress and long leaf pine at 32 inches DBH are Heritage), removal requires a permit and 1:1 DBH-inch replacement, and where live oaks are removed at least 50% of replanting must be live oak — though a tree removal permit is NOT required on a lot occupied by a single-family or two-family residence. The town separately adopted an ordinance amending Chapter 97 to add tree preservation and replacement requirements on 3 November 2025. (10) CAMA: development in a regulated Area of Environmental Concern requires a CAMA permit, and the final as-built survey must report impervious surface percentages and, inside an AEC, the impervious percentage within the AEC limits. (11) PET/VET BUSINESSES: animal pens must be enclosed in a building, overnight boarding must be at least 200 feet from any residential zoning district, all animal boarding operations must be air conditioned, and outdoor exercise runs are restricted to 8:00 AM–5:00 PM — meaning pet turf here skews INDOOR.
facts.turf_specifics: THE ONLY TOWN IN THIS BATCH WITH TWO GENUINELY DIFFERENT INSTALLATION ENVIRONMENTS, AND THE PAGE SHOULD SAY SO. ISLAND (roughly a third of the town): wind-deposited dune sand of the Newhan type — excessively drained, permeability around 20 inches per hour, water table 6 feet or deeper, and up to 35% calcareous shell fragments by volume. Drainage is a non-problem; the problems are base stability in loose sand, wind uplift at the perimeter, and constant salt spray and salt-laden groundwater. Fixation and edge detail matter far more than drainage here, and salt is a genuine argument FOR turf, since salt spray is what kills natural lawns on the strand. MAINLAND (the golf communities and the bulk of the housing): Leon-type coastal flatwoods — poorly to very poorly drained, spodic Bh hardpan within 30 inches, seasonal high water table sitting at 6–18 inches for several months a year, moderate-to-moderately-slow permeability through the pan. Exactly the opposite problem: water will not go down, so the base needs designed fall to a daylighted outlet. Selling the same base detail on both sides of the bridge is how installers get callbacks here. Additional island-specific constraints from the town code: the primary frontal dune is regulated and effectively off-limits to turf, solid plastic underlayment is prohibited outright, and rubberised infill and mulch products are restricted in the island zoning districts (see ordinance field). Logistics note: the island is reached by a single bridge — the old pontoon swing bridge served until 2010 and was replaced by the current arc bridge; the original now operates as a museum and gift shop. CAVEAT: soil series are USDA regional Official Series Descriptions, not verified parcel-level mapping.
facts.housing_stock: 5,066 housing units and 55.1% VACANT at the 2020 census — the defining number for this town and the highest vacancy in the batch by a wide margin. Roughly a third of the town's 7.88 sq mi sits on a barrier island between the Atlantic and the Intracoastal Waterway; the rest is mainland. Reported as approximately 1,200 homes across island and mainland neighbourhoods, with only about 100 full-time island residents — so the island is almost entirely second homes and vacation rentals, while the mainland golf-course communities hold the year-round retirees. Median age 68.0, the oldest in the batch; 60.1% of residents are 65 or older. Population 4,175 (2020), up from 3,572 (2010) and just 1,824 (2000). Development began in 1955 under Mannon C. Gore and the town incorporated in 1963, but the volume of stock is modern: the doubling from 2000 to 2020 means most houses are post-1990 golf-community and coastal product. Heavily HOA'd on the mainland through the golf plantations — Sea Trail Resort, Oyster Bay, Sandpiper Bay, Thistle. NOTE: typical lot sizes not verified this session; the '1,200 homes' figure and the 5,066 housing-unit count come from the same source and appear to describe different things (likely island-plus-mainland dwellings versus total census housing units) — reconcile before publishing a specific number.
facts.who_lives_there: Two distinct populations that need different copy. On the island: almost nobody full-time — roughly 100 year-round residents against a 55% vacancy rate, so the island is second-home owners and weekly renters, and the buyer is an absentee owner or a rental manager who cares about how the property shows and how little it needs while they are away. On the mainland: retirees in golf-course communities, primary residences, 60.1% over 65, median age 68. There is essentially no working-family population and no school in the town at all. The seasonal swing is the business reality — the customer is frequently not in North Carolina when the work is quoted, sold or installed, which argues for remote-friendly proposals, video walkthroughs and photo documentation as an actual service feature on this page.
facts.golf: The densest verified golf cluster in the batch, and all of it is named and checkable. SEA TRAIL GOLF RESORT — three separate championship courses in Sunset Beach, one each by Willard Byrd, Dan Maples and Rees Jones, playing through live oaks with Spanish moss and along the Calabash River. SANDPIPER BAY GOLF & COUNTRY CLUB — Sunset Beach, Dan Maples, 27 holes across the Sand, Piper and Bay nines. THISTLE GOLF CLUB — 1815 Olde Thistle Club Road, Sunset Beach, NC 28468; 27 holes named for Scottish clans (Cameron, MacKay, Stewart), with a clubhouse deliberately built to mimic a Scottish club grown over a century from the early 1800s. OYSTER BAY GOLF LINKS — named by the county tourism authority as a Sunset Beach course and as one of the town's golf communities, but its former domain is dead and I could not verify current operations; VERIFY BEFORE PUBLISHING. The tourism board credits Sunset Beach with six championship courses. Minutes away in Calabash: The Pearl, Brunswick Plantation, Farmstead, Meadowlands.
facts.commercial_targets: No school in town — the town's children attend schools in Shallotte and Ash. The realistic commercial inventory is resort, attraction and HOA rather than municipal: Sea Trail Resort (three courses plus resort grounds, villas and a conference operation — the largest single commercial ground in town); Sandpiper Bay Golf & Country Club; Thistle Golf Club at 1815 Olde Thistle Club Road, whose Scottish-heritage clubhouse and 27 holes make it a natural practice-green and clubhouse-surround prospect; Oyster Bay (verify status); Ingram Planetarium at 7625 High Market Street; the Old Bridge Museum; the Sunset Beach Pier; and the mainland golf-community HOAs as common-area buyers. The vacation-rental management companies are an underrated commercial channel here specifically because 55% of housing units are vacant and owners are absentee — one property manager can carry many installs. GAP: no named daycare, pet daycare, boarding or grooming business was verified for Sunset Beach; the session's search budget ran out. Note the town's own zoning makes overnight animal boarding hard to site (200 ft from residential, must be air conditioned), so indoor pet-facility turf is the likelier product than outdoor runs.
facts.landmarks: The Kindred Spirit Mailbox on undeveloped Bird Island, immediately west of Sunset Beach — walk-in only, and the single most recognisable local landmark. Bird Island itself. The Sunset Beach swing bridge, retired in 2010 and now the Old Bridge Museum and gift shop; the current arc bridge is the only vehicle access to the island. The Sunset Beach Pier, roughly 900 feet. Ingram Planetarium at 7625 High Market Street, Sunset Beach, NC 28468 — full-dome theatre, the Paul Dennis Science Hall, and laser shows, run by the Ocean Isle Museum Foundation alongside the Museum of Coastal Carolina in Ocean Isle Beach. Sea Trail Resort. Restaurants: Sarah's Kitchen, Oak & Palm Waterfront Dining, Fibber McGee's. Geographic bragging right worth using: Sunset Beach is the southernmost beach in North Carolina, with Ocean Isle Beach to its east and the South Carolina line just west.

name: Hickmans Crossroads

facts.strongest_angle: LEAD WITH NEW CONSTRUCTION AND THE BUILDER, NOT WITH RETIREMENT OR GOLF — that is what makes this page different from every neighbouring page and from what anyone would guess from the name. The parcel record says the median house within a mile of Hickmans Crossroads was finished in 2023 and that 524 of 941 structures went up in the 2020s, on 8,700-square-foot lots, with 177 townhomes, seven HOAs and eight builders still holding 470+ lots. This is not a sleepy crossroads and it is not the finished retirement product; it is the active construction frontier between Calabash and Ash, wrapped around The Meadowlands Golf Club. Open the page on the handover problem every one of these buyers is living through: a quarter-acre lot on compacted builder fill, sod laid over spoil, a five-foot side yard that never dries out, an HOA architectural committee that has to approve any change, and a county water restriction that lets a brand-new lawn drink only three nights a week for one inch total. Then make the second half explicitly B2B — model-home yards, townhome courtyards, amenity-centre dog parks and pool surrounds — and name the builders and associations: Coastal Club, Calabash Station, Springmill (Berkshire and Somerset), Meadowlands, Anderson Farms, Egret Landing, The Palms, Hickmans Crossing. Include the two technical hooks nobody else will: the county counts gravel and compacted earth as impervious surface but excludes a 4-inch #57-stone base over geotextile from built-upon area, which protects a small lot's BUA allowance; and the county's Stage 1 irrigation schedule explicitly names athletic fields and golf courses, which is the opening line for every club and HOA amenity conversation in the ring. HOW THIS DIFFERS FROM ITS NEIGHBOURS: Calabash and Carolina Shores proper are the FINISHED 2000s retirement product — median age 65.4, 3,297 units built 2000-2009, 15% second homes — so their pages are about renovation, downsizing and low-maintenance retirement yards. Sunset Beach is a barrier island with salt spray and CAMA rules. Little River is across a state line with different licensing, codes and HOA statutes. Ash, eight miles north, is farm country on 2-acre lots with no HOA at all. Hickmans Crossroads is the only one of them that is a construction site with a homeowners association, and it is the closest of this batch to the Myrtle Beach commercial work the owner is chasing. SERVICE AREA: comfortably INSIDE the client's polygon — 3 miles from Carolina Shores, 4 from Little River, 7 from the ocean. Of these four places, this is the one that unambiguously deserves a page.
facts.ordinance_or_hoa: BOTH LAYERS APPLY HERE, unlike the other three. HOA LAYER — seven named associations confirmed as owner-of-record on common-area parcels: Meadowlands POA Inc; Calabash Station Homeowners Association Inc; Spring Mill Plantation POA Inc; Coastal Club POA Inc and Coastal Club Property Owners Association Inc; Anderson Farm HOA Inc; Calabash Palms HOA Inc; Hickmans Crossing HOA Inc. 47 parcels carry the 'SFR CA' (common area) use code. On a 0.20-acre lot inside a platted subdivision, the ARC approval and the plat's built-upon-area allocation are usually the binding constraint, not the county — every job here needs the covenants checked first. COUNTY LAYER — the area is unincorporated, so the Brunswick County Stormwater Ordinance (eff. 9/16/2002, 'the unincorporated areas of the county are subject to the ordinance') and the UDO (revised 8/19/2024) apply. Sec. 1.16(b) requires a Stormwater Management Plan and County Stormwater Permit for 'All non-residential development' (b)(i) — directly relevant to a daycare, pet daycare or amenity-centre job; for 'Any filling or excavation of a parcel that results in a change of land surface of four (4) inches or more and alters the existing drainage pattern' (b)(iii); and for disturbance within 30 feet of a stream or natural waterway (b)(ii) — live in these pond-and-lagoon layouts. Sec. 1.6(p) counts 'compacted earth... [and] gravel' as impervious surface; Sec. 1.6(d) excludes from Built-upon Area 'a surface of number 57 stone, as designated by the American Society for Testing and Materials, laid at least four inches thick over a geotextile fabric' — which is how you keep a turf install from eating a lot's remaining BUA allowance. The UDO contains no artificial-turf provision. UDO 6.10 fence heights: RR/R-7500 6 ft front, 6 ft other, 8 ft with administrative adjustment; R-6000/SBR-6000/MR-3200 4 ft front, 6 ft other; commercial N-C 4/8/10, C-LD and C-I 6/8/10; 6.10.2.C bars fences that impede water flow in any swale or ditch, and 6.10.2.G asks that fences be built to survive hurricanes. CAVEAT TO VERIFY PER PARCEL: some of this area may fall in the Town of Calabash or Town of Carolina Shores ETJ; confirm jurisdiction on each address before quoting permit requirements. Burn ban for unincorporated Brunswick County since 6/8/2026.
facts.turf_specifics: USDA NRCS SSURGO returns 'Goldsboro fine sandy loam, 0 to 2 percent slopes' — 87% Goldsboro (moderately well drained, Aquic Paleudults), 7% Norfolk (well drained), 6% Lynchburg. Hydrologic group A/D; flooding frequency none; elevation 34 ft, the lowest of the four. BUT — and this is the practical point for a 2023-median-build subdivision — on 0.20-acre production-builder lots the native Goldsboro profile is largely gone. What a crew actually meets is compacted structural fill, builder's spoil and a thin sod layer, sitting on a pad graded for the house rather than for the yard. Treat the soil survey as context, not as what is under the shovel. Salt exposure: real but moderate — 7.0 miles to the Atlantic surf and 6.5 miles to the ICW, so salt aerosol and brackish groundwater influence, not direct spray; this is the inland side of the Calabash corridor, not an oceanfront exposure. Irrigation: this is the one of the four where the county water restriction genuinely bites, because these subdivisions are on Brunswick County water. Stage 1 Voluntary Water Conservation Alert in force (Stage 2 MANDATORY until June 9, 2026); county classified Extreme Drought (D3) per NCDMAC 9/3/2026 with Exceptional Drought (D4) in the SOUTHERN end of the county — which is here. The Stage 1 schedule: automatic irrigation limited to one inch per week, 8 p.m. to 4 a.m. only, odd-numbered addresses Tue/Thu/Sat nights and even-numbered addresses Wed/Fri/Sun nights, and the county states it applies to 'residential and commercial lawn and landscaping, ATHLETIC FIELDS, GOLF COURSES that do not use private groundwater wells or reclaimed water.' Brunswick County describes itself as USDA Hardiness Zone 8B / Coastal Plain.

name: Murrells Inlet

facts.strongest_angle:
LEAD WITH THE CREEK, NOT WITH GOLF. Every turf competitor in the Grand Strand leads with golf, and in Murrells Inlet that is the obvious, crowded, and weaker play. The page should open on the estuary: 16.5 miles of tidal creeks and 3,100 acres of shellfish beds, on the state's impaired-waters list for bacteria, with a 2005 TMDL and a 2014 watershed plan written to protect the oyster harvest that a 2022 audit says the county never implemented. Then the turn: your lawn is an input to that. Fertilizer, weed-and-feed, and irrigation runoff on a creek-side lot go into the same water the oysters filter and the restaurants sell. Synthetic turf, installed over a base that actually drains, takes that input to zero — and it does it on the pluff mud and brackish water table where sod has never held anyway. That gives the page a moral argument, a technical argument, and a maintenance argument in one paragraph, and it is unavailable to any other town on this list.

Second beat, not first: the 60.4 median age and 38.3% over-65. This is the client's highest-conversion residential demographic in the entire service area — retirees with golf money who are done mowing — and the backyard putting green sells itself once they've read the first section and trust the installer.

WHY IT DIFFERS FROM NEIGHBORS: Wampee and Hand are inland SC-90 sand-and-clay towns where the problem is compacted builder fill and a perched water table on land that was pine forest thirty months ago; Murrells Inlet is a salt-marsh estuary town where the problem is organic muck, tidal groundwater, salt aerosol, and a regulated watershed. Garden City Beach next door is seasonal rental; Murrells Inlet is year-round retiree. Pawleys Island to the south is old-money low-key; Murrells Inlet is a working waterfront with a nightlife strip. And the county line is a genuine content asset nobody else uses: the Murrells Inlet CDP is in GEORGETOWN County, but ZIP 29576 also covers the Horry County side (Garden City, Burgess, the St. James school cluster) — different county stormwater rules, different school district, different permit desk. A page that says 'tell us which side of the line you're on and here's what changes' will outrank and outconvert every templated competitor page in the market.
facts.ordinance_or_hoa: REAL and CHECKABLE, and it is a moving target as of the check date. (1) Georgetown County stormwater: every property in the county with 400 sq ft or more of impervious area pays a stormwater user fee. The county's own FAQ defines impervious surface as rooftops, driveways, patios, sidewalks, parking lots and other man-made structures resistant to infiltration — properly installed, free-draining synthetic turf over an open-graded aggregate base is not one of those listed items, but the county's 2014 Stormwater Management Ordinance defines impervious more broadly as a surface 'highly compacted or covered with a layer of material so that it is highly resistant to infiltration.' That ambiguity is worth addressing head-on on the page: build the base to drain, keep the documentation, and expect to have the conversation. Do NOT publish a flat 'turf is pervious in Georgetown County' claim without a written determination from the Stormwater Division (843-545-3524). (2) Land Disturbance Permit triggers at 0.5 acre if within 0.5 mile of a major water body, or 1 acre otherwise — most of Murrells Inlet residential work is under it, but commercial and multi-lot work is not. (3) NEW WETLANDS ORDINANCE IN PROGRESS: the Georgetown County Planning Commission voted 5–1 on 23 April 2026 to recommend a wetlands ordinance replacing the current 15-foot saltwater-wetland setback with a 35-foot minimum buffer from wetlands over half an acre, 50 feet where the wetland adjoins a water body, and 100 feet adjoining state parks/preserves/refuges, plus county approval before placing fill in wetlands over a quarter-acre. A commission member confirmed on the record it applies to development near Murrells Inlet's salt marsh. It needs three County Council votes and had not been adopted as of the check date — VERIFY STATUS BEFORE PUBLISHING. Existing structures, lots of record, forestry and farming are exempt, which matters: most turf jobs here are on existing lots of record. (4) HOA/ARB: the gated communities (Wachesaw Plantation, Prince Creek's sub-neighborhoods, Cypress River, Collins Creek) run architectural review boards — synthetic turf approval is per-community and per-board, not a county question. SC's 2018 HOA Act requires governing documents be recorded with the Register of Deeds, so covenants are actually retrievable — a genuine 'we pull your covenants before we quote' service differentiator.
facts.turf_specifics:
This is the only place in the batch where the SITE is the story. The Murrells Inlet Estuary runs ~5 miles behind the barrier beach, up to 1.5 miles wide, with 16.5 miles of tidal creeks and over 3,100 acres of shellfish beds, stretching from Huntington Beach State Park (Georgetown County) to Garden City Beach (Horry County). Consequences: (a) pluff mud and organic marsh muck within feet of grade on creek-side lots — base has to be built, not just graded, and geotextile separation is non-negotiable; (b) brackish, tidally-influenced shallow water table on the eastern half — a sub-base that holds water will pump fines and go soft; (c) direct salt aerosol exposure on the inlet and toward Huntington Beach — real UV+salt duty cycle on fibers and on any steel fastener, staples and nails should be spec'd accordingly; (d) inland/west of US 17 the ground flips to Waccamaw Neck sandy loams over the old rice fields — better infiltration but heavily compacted by 1990s–2000s construction fill.

The water-quality hook is the strongest technical selling point available anywhere in this service area: the estuary has sites on South Carolina's impaired-waters list for bacteria, a bacteria TMDL approved in 2005, and a Murrells Inlet Watershed Plan completed in 2014 specifically to protect local oyster harvests — which a 2022 audit found Georgetown County had failed to implement. A residential lawn on the creek is a fertilizer, pesticide and irrigation-runoff source feeding straight into shellfish beds. Turf removes that input. No other town on this list can make that argument.
facts.housing_stock:
CDP median construction year is 2002 — this is NOT an old fishing village housing stock, it is a 1990s–2000s golf-and-gated buildout wrapped around an 18th-century village core. 5,762 housing units; 57.2% detached single-family (rest is condo/townhome/villa, heavy along US 17 Bypass and the golf courses). 2020 census population 9,740 (up from 7,547 in 2010 — 29% growth in a decade); ~10,044 in 2024. Land area 7.32 sq mi, so ~752 people/sq mi — suburban, not rural, not dense. Three distinct stock types the page must speak to separately: (1) old inlet-front and creek-front lots off Business 17 / Wachesaw Road — irregular, mature live oaks, tiny to half-acre, no HOA, often raised or on fill; (2) gated golf communities on former rice plantations — Wachesaw Plantation, Wachesaw East, Prince Creek (Collins Creek, Collins Creek Landing, Highwood, Creek Harbour, Seasons), Blackmoor, Indigo Creek, Cypress River Plantation, Woodlake Village, The Hermitage — quarter- to half-acre, HOA-governed, mandatory ARB approval; (3) 55+ and low-maintenance villa product on the Bypass. HOA prevalence is HIGH on the west/inland side, near zero on the creek side. Mixed second-home/year-round: the CDP is much more year-round-retiree than Garden City Beach next door, which is genuinely seasonal-rental.

CAUTION FLAG: a widely-syndicated figure of $38,665 "median income" for Murrells Inlet is almost certainly median individual earnings, not median household income, and should NOT be put on the page — it reads as a poor town, which contradicts every other indicator (gated golf, 2002 median build, 60.4 median age). Get household income from Census QuickFacts directly before publishing any income claim.
facts.who_lives_there: Retirement-weighted year-round residents. Median age 60.4 (2024); 38.3% of the population is 65 or older — that is roughly double the SC state rate. Median age was 47 in 2010, so the community has aged more than a decade in fifteen years: this is an in-migration of retirees, not aging-in-place. Practical consequence for the client: the dominant buyer is a 60–75-year-old transplant (heavily Northeast/Midwest) who moved here for golf and the water, is on a fixed but comfortable budget, does not want to mow, does not want to hire a mow crew forever, and is the single most receptive demographic in the whole service area to a backyard putting green. Secondary: the working seafood/restaurant/charter economy along the MarshWalk (year-round employment, modest income, mostly renters — not a turf customer). Tourists are day-visitors to the MarshWalk, Brookgreen and Huntington Beach — they are not the audience, but they ARE why the commercial hospitality properties here care about how their grounds look.
facts.golf: Dense and all of it built on former rice/indigo plantation ground, which is why the fairway soils are what they are. In or immediately adjacent: TPC of Myrtle Beach (Tom Fazio, the only TPC course in South Carolina, inside Prince Creek; former host of the Senior PGA Tour Championship, now hosts Dustin Johnson's World Junior Golf Championship); Wachesaw Plantation Club (private, gated, Tom Fazio); Wachesaw Plantation East Golf Club (Clyde Johnston, hosted LPGA events); Blackmoor Golf Club (Gary Player, on a historic rice plantation along the Waccamaw); Indigo Creek Golf Club (built on a former rice and indigo plantation); The International Club of Myrtle Beach and Prestwick nearby to the north. Golf-community density is the highest of any town in this batch by a wide margin.
facts.commercial_targets: HIGHEST-VALUE TARGET IN THE BATCH FOR THE OWNER'S STATED GOAL: St. James High School, 10800 Highway 707, Burgess/Murrells Inlet 29576 (Horry County Schools) — 1,880 students, opened 2003, and the campus already has a 5,000-seat football/soccer stadium ringed by an eight-lane track, baseball AND softball fields, tennis courts, and an on-campus cross-country course. Eleven fall, seven winter, thirteen spring and five year-round sports on natural grass six miles from the ocean. That is the softball-field conversion pitch, with a name and an address. Also: St. James Middle School, 9775 St. James Road, Murrells Inlet 29576; St. James Elementary; Burgess Elementary; Seaside Elementary; St. Michael's Catholic School — a verified local childcare operator runs pickup routes from St. James Elementary, St. Michael's, Burgess Elementary and Seaside Elementary, which is a ready-made list of after-school-care play-area prospects. On the Georgetown County side, the adjacent Waccamaw Elementary / Intermediate / Middle / High cluster (Georgetown County School District, Pawleys Island) is a separate district with a separate procurement path — worth treating as two sales motions, not one. Tidelands Waccamaw Community Hospital is on the US 17 Bypass in Murrells Inlet (verify exact street address before publishing — tidelandshealth.org blocked automated retrieval on the check date). MarshWalk restaurants and tiki bars are legitimate small-commercial turf prospects: rooftop/deck bars, patio putting features, and shaded areas under live oaks where grass will never grow. Golf clubs above are commercial prospects for practice greens, tee lines and driving-range tees. Pet businesses: Murrells Inlet 29576 has an active pet-services market (grooming, boarding, dog-friendly MarshWalk patios) but I could NOT verify individual business names — Yelp and BringFido both refused automated retrieval on the check date. Do a manual Google Maps sweep for 'dog daycare / pet resort 29576' before naming anyone on the page.
facts.landmarks: Murrells Inlet MarshWalk — half-mile boardwalk over the salt marsh, roughly a dozen restaurants and tiki bars. Morse Park Landing — public waterfront, working docks, shrimp boats. Brookgreen Gardens, 1931 Brookgreen Drive — National Historic Landmark, founded 1931 by Archer and Anna Hyatt Huntington, largest collection of outdoor American figurative sculpture in the country. Huntington Beach State Park, directly across US 17 from Brookgreen — three miles of undeveloped Atlantic shoreline, loggerhead nesting, freshwater lagoon, and Atalaya Castle (the Huntingtons' Moorish Revival winter home). The Hot Fish Club — operating in some form since the 1700s, one of the oldest restaurants on the Grand Strand. Wicked Tuna and the Lip Rippin' Chilympics on the MarshWalk. Crazy Sister Marina and the charter fleet. Inlet Square Mall on the US 17 Bypass. The Murrells Inlet jetties (Corps project authorized 1971, completed 1980). 'Seafood Capital of South Carolina' is the self-applied tagline and locals use it unironically.

name: Pireway

facts.strongest_angle: LEAD WITH THE FLOOD AND WITH "NO RULES." This must not be a golf page and must not be a coastal page. THE LEAD: Pireway is river-bottom ground where the National Weather Service's own flood statements name your road. At 21 feet on the Waccamaw at Freeland, "Pireway RD between Horseshoe RD NW and Rivergate DR will be impassable"; at lower stages the warning reads "In North Carolina, River Road in Pireway may begin to flood." Florence put that gauge to a record 22.67 ft on 20 September 2018; Matthew hit 19.00 ft in 2016; it crested over 17 ft again in August 2024. A sod lawn on Torhunta / Muckalee / Croatan bottomland silts in, ruts and dies after every high water, and re-sodding is an every-few-years tax. The honest pitch here is a properly built, permeable, flood-survivable surface — an aggregate base that actually drains and a turf you hose off and get back — NOT a water-savings pitch, because most of these households are on their own well and nobody is telling them when they may irrigate. WHY IT DIFFERS FROM THE TOWN NEXT DOOR: twenty-five miles east at Brick Landing the constraints are regulatory and saline — a 30-foot CAMA buffer where the state actually banned artificial turf, brackish tidal marsh, a gate you cannot canvass, and a county irrigation schedule that cycled through three restriction stages in the summer of 2026. Pireway has none of that: no CAMA jurisdiction, no salt, no HOA, no gate, no restriction schedule. Just fresh blackwater that comes over the bank every few years, and a Columbus County floodplain development permit if you are inside the mapped SFHA. Loris, twelve miles southwest, is the same farm culture but in another state — different licensing, and no NC turf-is-not-impervious statute to lean on. So Pireway is the "no-rules, high-water, well-water, no-golf" page — the only one of its kind in the polygon, and genuinely un-templatable. A second, quieter angle worth one paragraph: the same region that set a flood record in 2018 was in Extreme Drought in July 2026 with Whiteville asking for voluntary conservation. Feast-or-famine water is the through-line, and turf is the only surface that ignores both. RESEARCH HONESTY FLAG FOR THE CLIENT: Pireway is by far the thinnest market in this batch — no census population, no commercial base, no golf, and it sits at the far inland corner of the drawn service area. It earns a short, honest page that captures a handful of long-tail queries and funnels to Tabor City / Whiteville / Ash — not a full-weight town page. Recommend building it at roughly half the length of a Shallotte or Ocean Isle page, and resist the urge to invent a housing profile or a local business list that does not exist.
facts.ordinance_or_hoa: WHAT DOES NOT APPLY IS AS USEFUL AS WHAT DOES. (1) NOT CAMA. Columbus County is not one of North Carolina's 20 CAMA coastal counties, so the 30-foot coastal shoreline buffer in which the Coastal Resources Commission banned artificial turf — the rule that governs Brick Landing and the whole Brunswick coast — has no application in Pireway at all. That is a clean, true, page-differentiating statement. (2) NO HOA REGIME. There is effectively no covenanted community here; that absence is itself the selling point relative to every other town on the map. (3) WHAT DOES APPLY — statewide: N.C.G.S. 143-214.7D(b)(6), enacted by S.L. 2024-49 (SB 166) Sec. 4.48, effective Sept 2024 and retroactive to July 2023 — artificial turf that is "manufactured to allow water to drain through the backing of the turf, [and] is installed according to the manufacturer's specifications over a pervious surface" is NOT built-upon area / impervious surface. (4) WHAT DOES APPLY — locally: the Columbus County Flood Damage Prevention Ordinance, originally enacted 17 March 1987 and carried in the county's Chapter 10 (Planning & Zoning), plus a Floodplain Development Permit for work in the mapped floodplain or floodway. Regrading and importing an aggregate base inside a Special Flood Hazard Area is precisely the class of activity that ordinance reaches. The county is actively enforcing floodway rules — it has posted formal notice that recreational vehicles are prohibited in designated floodway areas. Columbus County is also mid-way through a comprehensive Chapter 10 ordinance update (draft dated 16 June 2026) that changed the flood ordinance's valuation basis from assessed to market value for FEMA/NFIP alignment. FLAG: I could not retrieve turf-specific text from the Columbus County ordinance (the county PDFs blocked automated retrieval). Confirm scope with the Columbus County Planning Department before publishing any specific permit claim.
facts.turf_specifics: THE DEFINING FACT IS FLOOD, NOT SALT. The governing gauge is USGS 02109500 / NWS FREN7, "Waccamaw River at Freeland" (34.0950, -78.5483). Flood categories: Action 14 ft, Minor 15 ft, Moderate 18 ft, Major 19 ft; record 22.7 ft. The National Weather Service's own flood-impact statements name Pireway roads verbatim: at 21 ft, "Pireway RD between Horseshoe RD NW and Rivergate DR will be impassable"; at 22 ft and 22.7 ft, "Impassable or flooded roads include Rivergate DR, Pireway RD from Horseshoe RD NW to Rivergate DR, Mosquito Rd NW, Tripp TRL, Ash-Little River RD from Long RD NW to Hughes Smith RD, Ash-Little River RD near Pireway RD, Kingtown RD, Dock RD, and Crusoe Island RD..." Lower-stage NWS flood warnings read: "In North Carolina, River Road in Pireway may begin to flood." HISTORIC CRESTS: 22.67 ft on 09-20-2018 (Hurricane Florence — NHC and USGS record a new peak of record of 22.61 ft at 53,600 cfs on 19 Sept 2018, one of 28 flood records Florence set in the Carolinas); 19.30 ft on 09-21-1999 (Floyd); 19.00 ft on 10-12-2016 (Matthew — the Tabor-Loris Tribune reported evacuations in the River Road community near Pireway); 17.45 ft on 08-12-2024; 17.02 ft on 09-12-1996. Recent crests exceeded 15-16 ft in 2023 and 2024. This is a near-decadal, not once-in-a-lifetime, event. SOILS: NC DEQ's Brunswick County interbasin-transfer environmental assessment gives the Waccamaw study area "five major soil series: Torhunta, Woodington, Muckalee, Croatan, and Dorovan soils" — poorly drained loamy sands, floodplain soils and organic mucks. The 1953 topo of Pireway also shows Carolina bays (Marsh Bay, Jenrette Bay, Club Bay) — elliptical wet depressions with perched water and organic soil, a genuine base-prep problem. WATER TABLE: shallow; the whole corridor is bottomland. SALT: none — Pireway is roughly 25 miles inland and the Waccamaw here is fresh blackwater. That is the exact inverse of Brick Landing's constraint. IRRIGATION: Columbus County reached Extreme Drought (D3) by July 2026; the City of Whiteville issued a voluntary water conservation request effective 17 July 2026; as of May 2026 Columbus County News reported "No local governments have issued water restrictions, but all customers of municipal systems are urged to practice voluntary water conservation." FLAG: whether Pireway households specifically sit on a Columbus County numbered rural water district or on private wells is UNVERIFIED — the county operates numbered water districts, but I could not confirm coverage at Pireway. Verify before publishing.
facts.housing_stock: THIN PLACE — FLAG THIS TO THE CLIENT. Pireway is an unincorporated community in Columbus County at the junction of NC 904 and NC 905, elevation 39 ft, 34°01'38"N 78°38'16"W, formerly known as Pireway Ferry. It is not a CDP, has no census population, no ZIP of its own, and its Wikipedia article is a stub. There is no publishable housing dataset for Pireway specifically — any "median home value" or "population" figure on this page would have to be borrowed from Tabor City or Columbus County and should be labelled as such. WHAT IS VERIFIABLE: Pireway Road addresses carry Tabor City, NC 28463. Housing is rural and scattered — single-family houses and manufactured/modular homes on large acreage parcels along NC 904 (Pireway Rd), plus River Road, Rivergate Dr, Horseshoe Rd NW, Mosquito Rd NW and Tripp Trl down toward the Waccamaw. Farm and timber tracts; river camps along the water. No gated subdivisions and no HOA regime of any consequence. Listings on Pireway Rd, Tabor City run roughly $200k-$375k on acreage (e.g. 910 Pireway Rd, a 3-bed/1-bath 1,762 sq ft house, sold $230,000 on 10 Apr 2026; also 211 Pireway Rd and 20470 Seven Creeks Hwy). Historic building stock is catalogued in the Columbus County Architectural Survey (1998, NC State Historic Preservation Office), which lists Pireway Independent Church (CB-80) and houses along Pireway Road. HOA-HEAVY: no — essentially zero. SECOND-HOME: no. YEAR-ROUND: yes, almost entirely.
facts.who_lives_there: Year-round rural working households, farm and timber families, and retirees who never left. No tourism economy, no seasonal population, no second-home market — this is the inland farm-and-river corner of the drawn service polygon, not the coast. Commuting patterns run to Tabor City (8 mi NW), Whiteville (~25 mi N), Loris SC (~12 mi SW) and increasingly across the state line into the Myrtle Beach / North Myrtle Beach job market. FLAG: no verified demographic breakdown exists at the Pireway level; anything more specific must be cited to Columbus County or the Tabor City area and labelled as such.
facts.golf: NONE — and that is the point, not a gap. There is no golf course in Pireway and none in this corner of Columbus County. Every nearby course is across the state line in Horry County, SC: Diamondback Golf Club (Loris), Carolinas Country Club (Loris), Aberdeen Country Club (Longs) and Long Bay Club (Longs). Pireway is the one place in the entire service area where the golf-community frame is simply wrong. A backyard putting green here is a private hobby purchase for someone who drives 20-30 minutes to play, not an HOA- or community-driven one — and the page should be written that way.
facts.commercial_targets: THIN — DO NOT PAD THIS. There are no sports complexes, no daycares and no pet businesses in Pireway itself. Verified nearby/named: Pireway Community Church; Pireway Place Apartments (Tabor City); the Tabor City Visitors Center at Fifth St & Pireway Rd; and Pierce & Company, listed in the 1998 Columbus County architectural survey as still operating as a feed and general store (FLAG: current operating status unverified). SCHOOLS: Columbus County Schools serves the area and the Tabor City cluster is the realistic assignment, but FLAG — I could not verify Pireway's specific attendance zone; confirm with Columbus County Schools before naming a school on the page. HONEST RECOMMENDATION: the commercial targets for a Pireway page live in Tabor City (8 mi), Loris SC (12 mi) and Whiteville (25 mi), and the page should say so plainly rather than invent local businesses. For the owner's Myrtle Beach commercial ambition — municipal softball fields, daycares, pet daycares — Pireway contributes nothing. It is a residential long-tail page only.
facts.landmarks: Pireway Boating Access Area (NC Wildlife Resources Commission) on the Waccamaw River — the NC Administrative Code fixes its address as 9739 Pireway Road NW, Ash, and sets a no-wake zone for "the waters within 50 yards" of it; locals call it "Pireway landing off Hwy 904." The NC 904 Waccamaw River bridge, successor to the Pireway Ferry the place is named for. The NC 904 / NC 905 junction. Pireway Community Church and its cemetery, on the corner of NC 905. Pireway Independent Church (CB-80), catalogued in the 1998 Columbus County Architectural Survey. Seven Creeks Highway (NC 904 running west toward Tabor City) — the Revolutionary War Battle of Seven Creeks was fought near Pireway. The Tabor City Visitors Center, one of North Carolina's official welcome centers, at Fifth Street and Pireway Road in Tabor City. Crusoe Island Road and the Green Swamp; Nakina; Freeland and Ash just across the river in Brunswick County. The Shallotte / Nakina / Pireway / Ocean Isle Beach metric century (62-mile) loop in the Cape Fear Regional Bicycle Plan. And the NCDOT/Cape Fear RPO project to widen NC 904 to a multi-lane facility from US 17 to the Longwood Rd (SR 1321) / Pireway Rd intersection, programmed at $54,500,000. Cross-border note a local would catch: "Old Pireway Road" still exists in Horry County near Conway — the old road that ran to the ferry.

name: Brick Landing

facts.strongest_angle: LEAD WITH THE 30-FOOT COASTAL BUFFER AND THE 2026 DROUGHT — not with putting greens. Two things make this page unlike any other in the service area. First, this is the one NC place on the map where CAMA actually bites: because Brick Landing wraps the Intracoastal Waterway, waterfront and marsh-frontage owners CANNOT simply lay turf inside the 30-foot coastal shoreline buffer — the Coastal Resources Commission banned it 10-1 in 2021 and owners have to go get a variance. Everything outside that buffer, meanwhile, got dramatically easier in 2024: NC now says permeable-backed turf over a pervious base is not built-upon area, so on a 7,500 sq ft Co-R-7500 lot turf costs you nothing against your impervious allowance. A page that draws that line honestly — here is where you can, here is where you need a variance, and here is why your neighbour's installer got it wrong — is the most defensible local-authority page in the whole build. Second, the drought: Brunswick County spent summer 2026 cycling Stage 3 to Stage 2 to Stage 1 water restrictions under exceptional and extreme drought, with odd/even irrigation windows, while these same homeowners paid dues on a golf course that stayed green. The hero line writes itself. Third, tone: these residents literally bought their own golf course and re-sprigged fourteen greens with Sunday ultradwarf. Write to them like a superintendent — base depth, drainage, infill, salt tolerance at the marsh edge — not like a landscaper. WHY THIS DIFFERS FROM ITS NEIGHBOURS: Sunset Beach is an incorporated barrier-island retirement town with its own ordinance and oceanfront setbacks; Carolina Shores and Calabash are inland retiree towns with no waterway buffer problem at all; Shallotte is the commercial spine. Brick Landing's unique trio is estuarine-shoreline regulation + county (not town) jurisdiction + a member-owned golf course. PRACTICAL SALES NOTE FOR THE PAGE: the community is gated, 24/7 staffed, and posted "No Trespassing and No Solicitation" — so the page IS the front door here. There is no canvassing route into this neighbourhood; organic search and POA-member referral are the only ways in. HONEST GAPS: no population or home-count figure exists (not a CDP, not a census place); exact HOA covenant language on artificial turf is not public and must be requested from the POA at 910-755-3378 before any compliance claim is published.
facts.ordinance_or_hoa: FOUR REAL RULES, in order of usefulness. (1) NC G.S. 143-214.7D(b)(6), enacted by S.L. 2024-49 (SB 166) Sec. 4.48 — effective September 2024, retroactive to July 2023 — artificial turf is NOT built-upon area / impervious surface where it is "manufactured to allow water to drain through the backing of the turf, [and] is installed according to the manufacturer's specifications over a pervious surface." Statewide and binding on local jurisdictions. On a 7,500 sq ft Co-R-7500 lot in a coastal-stormwater county this is the whole ballgame: turf does not consume the lot's BUA allowance. (2) CAMA — the state Coastal Resources Commission voted 10-1 in September 2021 to PROHIBIT artificial turf within the 30-foot coastal shoreline buffer. Brick Landing fronts the AIWW, so waterway and marsh-frontage lots (Ship Wacche Estates deep-water lots especially) sit in an Estuarine Shoreline AEC and are hit by this. Owners have had to petition the CRC for variances to put turf in the 30-foot buffer (Carolina Beach petitioners were heard by the CRC in April 2025 and again November 2025). The CRC's 2025 rules review also included a clarification to 15A NCAC 07H .0209 that artificial turf is not considered landscaping. (3) Jurisdiction: Brunswick County zoning (Co-R-7500), not the Town of Ocean Isle Beach — permits go through the county. (4) HOA: Brick Landing HOA (910-755-3378) plus sub-associations including Mariner's Wacche Condo HOA; architectural approval expected. Gated, 24/7 security, and explicitly a "No Trespassing and No Solicitation Community." FLAG: the POA does not publish its covenants publicly and I could not retrieve any artificial-turf-specific covenant language. Do not publish an "HOA-approved" claim without calling the POA first.
facts.turf_specifics: SOILS: Brunswick County coastal-plain series. The county's own land use plan singles out Leon Fine Sand and Murville Mucky Fine Sand as the poorly drained/wet problem soils; Baymeade fine sand and Kureb are the well-drained sandy series; also Goldsboro, Rains, Torhunta, Foreston, Lumbee and Muckalee. Leon carries a spodic hardpan — water perches on it, which is exactly why a turf base here has to be engineered rather than scraped. County tables show Baymeade fine sand at 1–6% slope with depth to water table ~4.0–5.0 ft and severe limitations for some uses. WATER TABLE: high and seasonal across the Leon/Murville flats; the community sits on the tidal marsh edge. DRAINAGE: the golf course's own 2021 renovation had to include drainage work — a tell that this ground does not shed water on its own. SALT: yes — brackish tidal saltwater marsh and the AIWW run through the property; salt spray and brackish flood water are real, and this is the opposite of the inland towns on the map. IRRIGATION / WATER (the live hook, checked 2026-09-07): Brick Landing is on Brunswick County Public Utilities. 2026 drought timeline — Stage 1 Voluntary Water Conservation Alert issued June 9 2026 under Severe Drought (D2); escalated to a Stage 3 Water Shortage Warning under Exceptional Drought (D4), with automatic sprinklers cut to two days a week under a revised order ~Aug 10 2026; Stage 2 Mandatory around Aug 13 2026 as conditions improved to Extreme Drought (D3); back to Stage 1 Voluntary effective Aug 31 2026 with a recommended odd/even-address 8-hour irrigation window. As of early September 2026 the county is still in Extreme Drought with a burn ban in effect.

DOMINANT ERA: mid-1980s through 2000s, with active new-construction infill today — POA says "With lots still available, development continues." TYPE: single-family homes, townhomes and condominiums. name: Carolina Forest

facts.strongest_angle: LEAD WITH THE HOA APPROVAL PACKET, NOT THE YARD. Carolina Forest is unincorporated — there is no city, no local ordinance, and no permit counter to reassure anyone about. The gatekeeper is the architectural review committee, and every one of these 10,179 housing units sits inside a covenant community whose rules under SC Code § 27-30-130 must be recorded with the Horry County Register of Deeds and re-recorded every January 10 to be enforceable. So the page opens with something no other town's page can say: 'we submit to your ARC, and we can tell you whether your covenant actually bans this — most Carolina Forest covenants were written in the late 1990s and never mention artificial turf.' That is a specific, checkable, genuinely local promise. The rest of the page is the demographic: median age 39.6, 32.7% of households with children, 11.7% vacancy — small fenced back yards behind production-built houses, full of kids and dogs, on former International Paper pine flats where a spodic hardpan perches water 6 to 18 inches down for months at a time. Back-yard pet turf and small putting greens are the volume product here, and the golf-course subdivisions (Kingston Greens, Willow Greens, Inverness, River Oaks Golf & Tennis, Arrowhead Pointe) are the green-installation list. Then the institutional lead: two brand-new $60M+ elementary schools opened in August 2025 on Ronald McNair Blvd and Carolina Forest Blvd, with more construction signalled for the Highway 90 corridor. This is emphatically NOT the Myrtle Beach page (municipal softball conversion), NOT the North Myrtle Beach page (a new impervious-surface permit rule for absentee second-home owners), and NOT the Conway page (river flooding and slow loam). Carolina Forest is the batch's only page whose antagonist is a board, not a soil type or a city code. RESEARCH HONESTY: this is also the thinnest-documented of the four in one specific respect — as an unincorporated CDP first counted in 2020 it has no municipal records, and I could not reach Horry County's ordinances or read a single actual recorded covenant. Pull two or three Carolina Forest HOA covenants from the Horry County Register of Deeds before writing the compliance section.
facts.ordinance_or_hoa: THE KEY FACT IS JURISDICTIONAL: Carolina Forest is UNINCORPORATED. There is no Carolina Forest city hall, no Carolina Forest zoning ordinance and no Carolina Forest permit counter — land-use authority is Horry County, and the day-to-day gatekeeper on a turf installation is the architectural review committee of the individual HOA. Under SC Code § 27-30-130 an association's governing documents must be recorded with the Horry County Register of Deeds, and rules, regulations and amendments must be re-recorded annually by January 10 following adoption or amendment to remain enforceable; associations must also make rules available to members on request by email, common-area posting or website. That gives a genuinely useful, verifiable line for this page: if a board tells a homeowner artificial turf is prohibited, the prohibition has to be on record at the Register of Deeds — and a lot of covenants written in 1998 predate modern turf entirely and simply do not address it. RESEARCH GAPS, FLAG BOTH: (1) horrycountysc.gov was unreachable from this session on 2026-09-07, so I could not read Horry County's zoning ordinance, landscaping/open-space standards, fence heights, stormwater ordinance or ERU fee — all of that must be obtained before the page makes a compliance claim; (2) I did not obtain the actual recorded covenants for Waterbridge, Plantation Lakes, The Farm, Clear Pond, Berkshire Forest or Avalon, so I cannot say what any specific HOA's turf language is. Pulling two or three of those from the Register of Deeds would be the single highest-value piece of follow-up research in this batch.
facts.turf_specifics: Built on former commercial pine timberland — longleaf pine forests and savannas dotted with Carolina bays, the elliptical closed depressions that hold water. That origin is the whole turf story. Coastal-flatwoods soils of the Leon type dominate this landscape: very poorly to poorly drained sandy marine sediment with a spodic (Bh) hardpan within 30 inches of the surface and a seasonal water table at 6 to 18 inches for 1 to 4 months in most years. On a flatwoods lot the hardpan perches water and a turf base laid on top of it becomes a bathtub — the base has to be cut through or drained past it. HONEST CAVEAT: I verified the Leon series characteristics and I verified Carolina Forest's pre-development land cover, but I did NOT obtain a Carolina-Forest-specific NRCS soil survey; treat the hardpan as a flatwoods pattern to test per lot, not as a published finding. Add to that: subdivisions here were graded and filled, so the imported fill on any given lot may behave nothing like the native profile, and many communities are built around retention lakes with high adjacent water tables. Salt exposure is negligible — roughly five miles inland, no spray. The site was also the Conway Bombing and Gunnery Range in WWII, which is a real reason to be careful about deep excavation and to say so.
facts.housing_stock: 2020 census (its FIRST appearance as a CDP — it was not separately counted before 2020): 23,342 residents across 17.29 sq mi, 8,991 households, 10,179 housing units, only 11.7% vacant (homeowner vacancy 2.5%, rental vacancy 11.8%). Median age 39.6 — the family-formation age of the batch. 23.2% under 18, 18.2% over 65, and 32.7% of households have children under 18; 52.1% married-couple households. This is the batch's true residential-volume town and its housing is a single coherent product: master-planned, production-builder subdivisions built from roughly 1997 onward on land International Paper had held since acquiring the 30,000-acre Buist Tract in 1937. Carolina Forest Boulevard was completed December 1996 and River Oaks Drive December 1997, and the whole thing was built to a master plan negotiated between International Paper and Horry County. Typical product: 2–5 bedroom detached houses and townhomes on modest, uniform lots with small fenced back yards, plus a heavy amenity package (pools, clubhouses, lakes). HOA-heavy is an understatement — the association landscape here includes some of the largest and most complex residential communities in Horry County, several gated with access control, several with lakes and boat docks. ZIP 29579.
facts.who_lives_there: Year-round working families and relocating retirees, not tourists and not second-home owners. The 11.7% vacancy rate is the lowest in the batch and roughly one fifth of North Myrtle Beach's — almost nobody here is absent nine months a year. Racial composition 78.4% White, 8.0% Black, 2.8% Asian, 7.5% two or more races, 7.3% Hispanic/Latino. Buyers have come disproportionately from the Northeast and Midwest, drawn by the schools, newer housing and coastal proximity without oceanfront exposure. Practically: two-income households with kids and dogs, five miles from the beach, who bought into a covenant community on purpose and who will not install anything their architectural review committee hasn't approved.
facts.golf: Carolina Forest is ringed by 501-corridor golf rather than containing a signature course. Verified as being in or immediately adjacent to the CDP: Legends Golf Resort (multi-course) and Burning Ridge, both named as Carolina Forest-area places in Horry County Schools' own attendance-area descriptions; Myrtle Beach National; World Tour Golf Links; Arrowhead Country Club, 1201 Burcale Rd (27 holes on the Intracoastal, in the River Oaks/Burcale attendance area); River Oaks Golf Plantation (its subdivisions — River Oaks Golf & Tennis, Fairways at River Oaks, Waterway Village @ River Oaks — appear in the school attendance list); Man O' War and The Wizard on the 501 corridor. Wild Wing Plantation sits between Carolina Forest and Conway. Note the golf-course-adjacent subdivision names in the attendance list — Kingston Greens, Willow Greens, Willow Trace, Inverness, St. Andrews Townhomes, Grand Villas — every one of them is a household that already lives on a golf course and is the natural buyer for a backyard putting green.

TWO BRAND-NEW $60M+ ELEMENTARY SCHOOLS, OPENED AUGUST 2025 — the freshest capital projects in the batch. Both 1,200-student capacity, both designed by SMHa (Stubbs Muldrow Herin architects) with Thompson Turner Construction as contractor; names, mascots and colours approved by the Horry County Board of Education on 18 November 2024 and attendance lines finalised 9 December 2024. OTHER: Carolina Forest Recreation Center; The Hulk bike and run park; the amenity centres of Waterbridge, Plantation Lakes, Berkshire Forest, The Farm and Clear Pond (pools, tennis, pickleball, bocce, basketball and volleyball courts — every one of those is a common-area turf opportunity sold to a board, not a homeowner); Tanger Outlets and the Carolina Forest Blvd retail strip. name: Civietown

facts.strongest_angle: LEAD WITH INSTITUTIONS AND MUD — NOT GOLF, NOT SALT, NOT RETIREES. Civietown is the inland, working, year-round half of Brunswick County and every number says so: the youngest population in the batch (median age 55.4 versus 68.0 at Seaside), the cheapest housing ($253,000 versus $463,200 at Grissettown), the oldest housing stock (median built 1993), the largest lots (RR zoning, 20,000 sf minimum without utilities), no HOA density, and no golf course within 5.9 miles. Writing this page like a beach page would be transparently fake to anyone who lives here. Instead it is the page that chases the owner's actual commercial ambition on the North Carolina side of the line: it is the only one of the four ringed by public institutions — West Brunswick High School 5.3 mi, Supply Elementary 4.7 mi, Brunswick Community College 6.6 mi, Cedar Grove Middle, Virginia Williamson Elementary, Lockwoods Folly Township Park 4.2 mi, Shallotte Township District Park 7.0 mi, and a PetSmart in Shallotte. So it leads with school and municipal athletic fields, batting cages and bullpens, and multi-use practice space, with big-lot residential pet turf as the domestic counterpart. The technical hook that is TRUE ONLY HERE: Civietown's soils are the most varied of the four — Blanton, a Grossarenic Paleudult (deep leached sand over loam), and Kureb and Baymeade ridges with a 48-inch water table, alternating with Murville, Pantego and Torhunta swales where the water table is AT the surface. That mosaic is precisely why rural lots here have a dry patch and a permanent mud hole, and why gates, dog runs and dugout mouths turn to soup. And unlike the coastal three, salt is irrelevant — do not use it. Finally, Civietown is the only page that should mention the Lockwood Folly River basin, the shellfish beds and the county's Water Quality Protection overlay (25% built-upon cap, 30 ft wetland buffer, 75 ft from mean high water, within 575 ft of MHW, parcels under an acre exempt) — carefully framed as basin context and a parcel-check, since the mapped overlay is downriver. WHY THIS DIFFERS FROM ITS NEIGHBOURS: Grissettown sells putting greens to golf money, Thomasboro sells low-maintenance lawns to full-time retirees on wet flatwoods, Seaside sells salt-and-marsh survivability to absentee second-home owners. facts.ordinance_or_hoa: Unincorporated, county-governed, and this is the one town in the batch with a watershed-specific overlay worth naming. Civietown lies in the Lockwood Folly River basin — the only watercourse for which Brunswick County wrote a dedicated Water Quality Protection (WQP) Overlay, adopted to protect naturally occurring shellfish beds and incorporating by reference the 1989 'Lockwood Folly River Basin Water Quality Evaluation Report.' Where the WQP applies, development must 'Limit the built upon impervious area to no more than 25% of the lot,' provide a buffer of at least 30 ft from any wetland or water line, and keep structures at least 75 ft from the mean high water line; the overlay extends 575 ft landward of mean high water, and parcels under one acre are exempt. IMPORTANT ACCURACY NOTE: the WQP's mapped extent is the lower river — from Genoes Point to Mullet Creek, south to and across the Intracoastal Waterway to Sheep Island — so Civietown, well upriver, is probably NOT inside the overlay itself. Say 'you are in the basin the county singled out' and 'confirm your parcel against the WQP overlay map', not 'you are in the overlay'. The Lockwood Folly River is also a designated Viewshed Protection Overlay watercourse (300 ft from normal high water). facts.strongest_angle: LEAD WITH THE FOUR-INCH RULE AND THE DITCH — the unincorporated-county compliance page. Freeland has no HOA, no golf, no covenants and no county water for many households; what it has is two-acre lots, private wells, septic fields, roadside ditches, and a county stormwater ordinance that most installers have never read. The page should open on the one thing a Freeland landowner cannot Google an answer to: in unincorporated Brunswick County, excavating four inches or more and altering the existing drainage pattern triggers a County Stormwater Permit, and the county's own definition counts gravel and compacted earth as impervious surface while expressly excluding a #57-stone base four inches thick over geotextile from built-upon area. That is a genuinely differentiated, checkable, expensive-to-get-wrong claim. The secondary lead is mud, not luxury: 44% of the ZIP's housing is manufactured homes and the median home value is $198,100 — the sellable job here is a pet run, a mud-free entry pad and a dog yard beside a mobile home on acreage, not a $30k putting green. NOTE THE DIFFERENCE FROM NEIGHBOURS: Ash (4 mi) is the postal and civic centre and should carry the school/park content; Longwood and Pireway are the same rural fabric but sit closer to the Loris corridor; Calabash and Carolina Shores 15 miles south are a different planet (median age 65.4, HOA subdivisions, eleven golf courses). SERVICE-AREA FLAG: Freeland at 34.107 N sits roughly 4.7 miles north-northwest of Ash and about 5-7 miles north of a straight Shallotte-to-Loris line. It is a defensible fringe inclusion given the client's map clearly contains Ash and Pireway, but it is at the outer edge. SEO FLAG: Freeland, Exum and Makatoka all share ZIP 28420 (Ash) and the same ~1,145-parcel, ~2,658-person postal area with identical soil, zero HOAs and no golf. Three separate town pages would be three near-duplicates cannibalising each other. Recommend ONE strong 'Ash & Waccamaw Township' page naming Freeland, Exum, Makatoka, New Britton, Myrtle Head and Little Prong inside it — or, if separate pages are required, make Freeland the substantive one and keep the others as short satellites.
facts.ordinance_or_hoa: No HOA exists here (zero HOA/POA parcels countywide-north). The binding rules are the county's, and they apply precisely because Freeland is UNINCORPORATED. (1) BRUNSWICK COUNTY STORMWATER ORDINANCE (effective Sept. 16, 2002; 'the unincorporated areas of the county are subject to the ordinance'). Section 1.16(b) requires a Stormwater Management Plan and County Stormwater Permit for, among others: '(iii) Any filling or excavation of a parcel that results in a change of land surface of four (4) inches or more AND alters the existing drainage pattern' (septic exception aside); '(ii) Any activity that disturbs land within 30 feet of the banks of a stream or other natural waterway'; '(i) All non-residential development'; and '(iv)' anything disturbing one acre or more, except activity on a bona fide farm unless for non-farm purposes. A standard turf install excavates 3-4+ inches for base — this trigger is live, and the conjunctive 'and alters the existing drainage pattern' is the design lever. (2) The same ordinance's definitions are decisive for turf: Sec. 1.6(p) 'Impervious Surface. Any surface which in whole or in part, restricts or prevents the natural absorption of water into the ground. Such surfaces may include, but not be limited to, compacted earth (such as marl and coquina), GRAVEL, concrete, asphalt...' — i.e. a conventional compacted crusher-run base reads as impervious. But Sec. 1.6(d) 'Built-upon Area or BUA... does not include... a surface of number 57 stone, as designated by the American Society for Testing and Materials, laid at least four inches thick over a geotextile fabric.' An open-graded ASTM #57 stone base 4+ inches over geotextile is expressly excluded from BUA. That is a buildable spec, written into the county's own ordinance. (3) BRUNSWICK COUNTY UDO (readopted 3/16/2015, last revised 8/19/2024) contains NO artificial or synthetic turf regulation at all — verified by full-text search of the 19,000-line ordinance. Fences (UDO 6.10): RR / R-7500 districts 6 ft front yard, 6 ft other yards, 8 ft with administrative adjustment; fences do not require a building permit (UDO 3.1.4) but 6.10.2.C states 'Fences or walls shall not alter or impede the natural flow of water in any stream, creek, drainage swale, or ditch' — directly relevant to dog runs beside a roadside ditch. RR minimum lot area is 30,000 sq ft. (4) Burn ban in effect for unincorporated Brunswick County since June 8, 2026.
facts.turf_specifics: USDA NRCS Soil Data Access (SSURGO), point query: map unit is 'Goldsboro fine sandy loam, 0 to 2 percent slopes' — 87% Goldsboro (moderately well drained, Fine-loamy siliceous subactive thermic AQUIC Paleudults), 7% Norfolk (well drained, Typic Kandiudults), 6% Lynchburg (somewhat poorly drained). Hydrologic group A/D — behaves as group A where drained, group D (near-zero infiltration) where not. Flooding frequency: none. Minimum annual water table depth recorded as 0 cm, i.e. the seasonal high water table reaches the surface in undrained conditions. 'Aquic' in the taxonomy is the whole story: a sandy loam surface over a loamy subsoil that perches water. It drinks fast for the first 8 inches then stops. Salt exposure: negligible — 16.3 miles to the Atlantic shore, 15.2 miles to the ICW, no tidal water. Elevation 38 ft. Drainage here is roadside and field ditches, not storm sewer; the ditch IS the drainage system. Irrigation: Brunswick County is under a Stage 1 Voluntary Water Conservation Alert and was under Stage 2 MANDATORY restrictions until June 9, 2026; the county remains classified Extreme Drought (D3) as of the NC Drought Management Advisory Council update of Sept. 3, 2026, with Exceptional Drought (D4) in the south of the county. facts.strongest_angle: LEAD WITH COMMERCIAL HOSPITALITY, NOT RESIDENTIAL — this is the one town in the batch where the primary customer is a business. Calabash has about 2,011 residents and roughly thirty restaurants, a ratio that has held since the New York Times counted 32 restaurants and 180 residents here in 1983. The buyer is a restaurant owner with an entry, a patio and a waterfront deck that thousands of tourists cross every summer, in salt air, where natural grass dies and mud gets tracked inside; and the pitch is hard-wearing, drainable, salt-tolerant surfacing that looks the same in August as in May. Second pillar: this is a golf-resort town, with The Pearl, Brunswick Plantation, Farmstead, Meadowlands and Crow Creek all inside town or minutes out — which makes backyard and villa putting greens a natural, and gives you the batch's best story to open on. Farmstead's 18th is a 767-yard par 6 that begins in South Carolina and ends in North Carolina. Use it: a hole that crosses the state line is the perfect way to say, in one line, that this company works both sides of it and knows that NC licensing, NC stormwater rules and Brunswick County permitting start right here. WHY THIS DIFFERS FROM ITS NEIGHBOURS: Carolina Shores, which Calabash split from in 1998 and whose boundary still interlocks with it, is inland, waterless, ten years older on median age and governed by HOA architectural review — a residential approvals page. Sunset Beach is a barrier island with a hard 45% impervious cap, a 200-square-foot permit trigger and a PE certification standard — a regulatory competence page. Shallotte is a working family and school town with a one-acre threshold — a commercial-institutional page. Calabash is a working waterfront and hospitality town on a tidal river that drains into South Carolina — a restaurant, resort and putting-green page. Four adjacent towns, four genuinely different leads. FLAG FOR THE CLIENT: Calabash's own ordinances could not be retrieved this session and must be checked before any regulatory claim goes on this page.
facts.ordinance_or_hoa: HONEST GAP — I HAVE NOTHING VERIFIED AND WILL NOT INVENT IT. The Town of Calabash's website (townofcalabash.net) returned HTTP 403 to every method attempted this session, including a real browser, so I could not retrieve the town's zoning ordinance, impervious surface limits, stormwater thresholds, fence rules or landscaping standards. Treat Calabash's town-level regulation as UNRESEARCHED. What can be said with confidence and sourcing: Calabash is in Brunswick County, one of North Carolina's CAMA coastal counties, so development within a regulated Area of Environmental Concern — which will include tidal Calabash River frontage — requires a CAMA permit from the Division of Coastal Management or a designated local permit officer. Brunswick County's own Stormwater Quality Management and Discharge Control Ordinance also applies countywide. And a useful contextual precedent: neighbouring Sunset Beach caps residential impervious surface at 45% of lot area and triggers a stormwater plan at a 200-square-foot increase, while Shallotte triggers only at one acre — the range across adjacent Brunswick towns is enormous, so nothing should be assumed for Calabash by analogy. ACTION BEFORE PUBLISHING: retrieve the Calabash zoning ordinance directly from Town Hall or a normal browser session, and check specifically for impervious/built-upon limits, any pervious-material certification path, and fence height rules. Also worth knowing for the page's credibility: Calabash and Carolina Shores separated in 1998 after 'years of bickering over sewer, garbage collection and sign restrictions,' and their boundaries still interlock — so an address's actual jurisdiction genuinely needs checking here.
facts.turf_specifics: A tidal, brackish, cross-border drainage town. Calabash sits on the tidal Calabash River, which flows to the Atlantic through South Carolina's Little River Inlet — so the town's water physically leaves North Carolina before it reaches the ocean, and riverfront properties sit on brackish tidal influence with real salt exposure on docks, decks and waterfront patios. Inland from the river the pattern is standard mainland coastal flatwoods: Leon-type soils, poorly drained, with a spodic Bh hardpan within 30 inches and a seasonal high water table at 6–18 inches for months at a time, so subgrade percolation cannot be assumed and turf base needs designed fall to an outlet. The commercially important surfaces in this town are not lawns at all — they are restaurant entries, waterfront decks, patios and dock approaches carrying very heavy seasonal foot traffic in a salt environment, which changes the spec toward higher face weight, UV and salt tolerance, drainage through the backing, and fixation detail on hard surfaces rather than over soil. Note also that this is the batch's cross-border town: work here sits in North Carolina under NC contractor licensing and Brunswick County permitting, minutes from an SC line where all of that changes. CAVEAT: soil series are USDA regional descriptions, not parcel-level mapping; no Calabash-specific soil or water-table data was obtainable this session.
facts.housing_stock: 1,546 housing units with 35.8% vacant — squarely between year-round Carolina Shores (15.8%) and vacation-rental Sunset Beach (55.1%), and the signature of a town that is part retirement, part seasonal, part working waterfront. Population 2,011 (2020), the smallest in the batch. Median age 56.4 with 32.9% aged 65 or older and 12.9% under 18 — and this is the surprise worth building on: Calabash is roughly TEN YEARS YOUNGER than Carolina Shores (66.0) and Sunset Beach (68.0), the towns it directly abuts. It is not a retirement town in the way its neighbours are. The stock is genuinely mixed by era in a way the others are not: a small historic fishing-village core on the Calabash River (the town had roughly 180 residents as recently as 1983), plus modern golf-resort and subdivision product built out as the population grew tenfold to about 2,000. Town boundaries interlock confusingly with Carolina Shores following the 1998 split. NOTE: typical lot sizes and HOA prevalence NOT verified this session — the town's website blocked every access attempt.
facts.who_lives_there: A working hospitality town with a retirement fringe, which is a different animal from its neighbours. The 56.4 median age and 12.9% under-18 share mean there are real working-age households here — the people who staff roughly thirty restaurants, crew the fishing and tour fleet, and run the shops. Layered on top: seasonal and second-home owners (35.8% vacancy) and golf-resort residents at Brunswick Plantation, The Pearl and Crow Creek. And layered on top of that, the actual economic engine — tourists, in enormous numbers relative to a town of 2,011, drawn by 'Seafood Capital of the World' branding that has held since the 1930s. The New York Times reported in 1983 that Calabash had 32 restaurants and about 180 residents; by 2023 the restaurant count was similar while the population had grown to roughly 2,000. A town with more restaurant seats than residents is a commercial market wearing a residential costume.
facts.golf: Verified and dense — five of the region's 30-plus courses are in Calabash per the county tourism authority. THE PEARL GOLF LINKS — 1300 Pearl Blvd, Calabash, NC 28467; Dan Maples, 1987; East, West and North nines laid through the woods and marshes of the Calabash River. facts.commercial_targets: THE STRONGEST COMMERCIAL DENSITY PER CAPITA IN THIS BATCH — roughly thirty restaurants against 2,011 residents.
